Of course. Aligning a table caption to the left without using the `caption` package is a classic LaTeX challenge. The default behavior of most document classes is to center the caption.

There are two primary ways to achieve this:

1.  **Redefining the internal caption macro.** This is the most robust method as it preserves all counter and cross-referencing functionality.
2.  **Creating a "manual" caption.** This is a more brute-force approach that is sometimes useful for a single, specific table.

Here are the details for both methods.

---

### Method 1: Redefining the Internal Caption Macro (Recommended)

This is the cleanest solution. LaTeX uses an internal macro called `\@makecaption` to format the caption's appearance. We can redefine it to align the text to the left instead of centering it. Because the macro name contains an `@` symbol, you must wrap the redefinition in `\makeatletter` and `\makeatother`.

Simply place this code in your document's preamble (before `\begin{document}`):

```latex
\makeatletter
\long\def\@makecaption#1#2{%
  \vskip\abovecaptionskip
  \sbox\@tempboxa{\textbf{#1:} #2}%
  \ifdim \wd\@tempboxa >\hsize
    \textbf{#1:} #2\par
  \else
    \global \@minipagefalse
    \hb@xt@\hsize{\box\@tempboxa\hfil}%
  \fi
  \vskip\belowcaptionskip}
\makeatother
```

**Explanation:**
*   The original definition typically contains `\hfil\box\@tempboxa\hfil`, which places flexible space on both sides, thus centering the content.
*   Our new definition uses `\box\@tempboxa\hfil`, which puts the content box first and then fills the rest of the line with flexible space, effectively pushing the caption to the left.
*   I've also made the caption label (`Table 1:`) bold with `\textbf{#1:}` for better visual distinction, which is a common style. You can remove `\textbf{}` if you prefer the standard, non-bold label.

#### Complete Example

```latex
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{lipsum} % For dummy text

% --- Preamble Code to Left-Align Captions ---
\makeatletter
\long\def\@makecaption#1#2{%
  \vskip\abovecaptionskip
  \sbox\@tempboxa{\textbf{#1:} #2}%
  \ifdim \wd\@tempboxa >\hsize
    \textbf{#1:} #2\par
  \else
    \global \@minipagefalse
    \hb@xt@\hsize{\box\@tempboxa\hfil}%
  \fi
  \vskip\belowcaptionskip}
\makeatother
% -------------------------------------------

\begin{document}

\section{Introduction}

\lipsum[1]

\begin{table}[h!]
  \centering
  \caption{This is a short caption that will now be aligned to the left.}
  \label{tab:short_caption}
  \begin{tabular}{|l|c|r|}
    \hline
    Header 1 & Header 2 & Header 3 \\
    \hline
    A & B & C \\
    D & E & F \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

As seen in Table~\ref{tab:short_caption}, the caption is on the left.

\begin{table}[h!]
  \centering
  \caption{This is a much longer caption designed to demonstrate how the text wraps. The entire block of text will be justified and aligned to the left margin, which is the desired behavior for multi-line captions in this style.}
  \label{tab:long_caption}
  \begin{tabular}{|c|c|}
    \hline
    Column A & Column B \\
    \hline
    Data 1 & Data 2 \\
    Data 3 & Data 4 \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\lipsum[2]

\end{document}
```
This change will aﬀect all captions (for both figures and tables) throughout your document.

---

### Method 2: Creating a Manual Caption

This method avoids redefining core commands but requires more manual work for each table. You essentially build the caption from scratch.

**Steps:**
1.  Use `\refstepcounter{table}` to correctly increment the table number so `\label` and `\ref` work.
2.  Use `\addcontentsline{lot}{table}{...}` to manually add an entry to the List of Tables.
3.  Format the caption text using `\tablename` (which prints "Table") and `\thetable` (which prints the number).
4.  Wrap everything in a `\parbox` or `minipage` to control its width and prevent a page break.

#### Complete Example

```latex
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{lipsum} % For dummy text

\begin{document}

\listoftables
\clearpage

\section{Introduction}

\lipsum[1]

\begin{table}[h!]
  \centering
  % The actual table content
  \begin{tabular}{|l|c|r|}
    \hline
    Header 1 & Header 2 & Header 3 \\
    \hline
    A & B & C \\
    D & E & F \\
    \hline
  \end{tabular}
  
  \vspace{5pt} % Manually add some space above the caption
  
  % --- Manual Caption ---
  \parbox{\linewidth}{%
    \refstepcounter{table}% Increment table counter
    \addcontentsline{lot}{table}{\protect\numberline{\thetable}My manual left-aligned caption}% Add to List of Tables
    \textbf{\tablename~\thetable:} My manual left-aligned caption\label{tab:manual_caption}% Create the caption text and label it
  }
  % --------------------
\end{table}

As you can see in Table~\ref{tab:manual_caption}, this also works.

\lipsum[2]

\end{document}
```

**Key parts of the manual method:**
*   `\refstepcounter{table}` **must** come before `\label`.
*   The `\parbox{\linewidth}{...}` ensures the caption text uses the full line width available and wraps correctly, while keeping it all together.
*   You lose the automatic spacing (`\abovecaptionskip`), so you may need to add manual space (e.g., `\vspace{5pt}`) as shown.

### Which Method Should You Use?

*   **Use Method 1** if you want all captions in your document to be left-aligned and you are comfortable placing code in your preamble. It is the most elegant and "correct" way to do it without an external package.
*   **Use Method 2** if you only need to change a single caption or if you are forbidden from modifying the preamble in a restrictive template. It is more work but is self-contained within the `table` environment.
